{{Short description|Limit on the parameters of a block code}}
In [[mathematics]] and [[computer science]], in the field of [[coding theory]], the '''Hamming bound''' is a limit on the parameters of an arbitrary [[block code]]: it is also known as the '''sphere-packing bound''' or the '''volume bound''' from an interpretation in terms of [[Sphere packing|packing balls]] in the [[Hamming metric]] into the [[Space (mathematics)|space]] of all possible words.  It gives an important limitation on the [[efficiency]] with which any [[error-correcting code]] can utilize the space in which its code words are embedded. A code that attains the Hamming bound is said to be a '''perfect code'''.

==Background on error-correcting codes==

An original message and an encoded version are both composed in an alphabet of ''q'' letters. Each code word contains ''n'' letters. The original message (of length ''m'') is shorter than ''n'' letters. The message is converted into an ''n''-letter codeword by an encoding algorithm, transmitted over a noisy [[communication channel|channel]], and finally decoded by the receiver. The decoding process interprets a garbled codeword, referred to as simply a ''word'', as the valid codeword "nearest" the ''n''-letter received string.

Mathematically, there are exactly ''q''<sup>''m''</sup> possible messages of length ''m'', and each message can be regarded as a [[coordinate vector|vector]] of length ''m''. The encoding scheme converts an ''m''-dimensional vector into an ''n''-dimensional vector. Exactly ''q''<sup>''m''</sup> valid codewords are possible, but any one of ''q''<sup>''n''</sup> words can be received because the noisy channel might distort one or more of the ''n'' letters when a codeword is transmitted.

== Statement of the bound ==
===Preliminary definitions===
An alphabet set <math>\mathcal{A}_q</math> is a set of symbols with <math>q</math> elements. The set of strings of length <math>n</math> on the alphabet set <math>\mathcal{A}_q</math> are denoted <math>\mathcal{A}_q^n</math>. (There are <math>q^n</math> distinct strings in this set of strings.) A <math>q</math>-ary block code of length <math>n</math> is a subset of the strings of <math>\mathcal{A}_q^n</math>, where the alphabet set <math>\mathcal{A}_q</math> is any alphabet set having <math>q</math> elements. (The choice of alphabet set <math>\mathcal{A}_q</math> makes no difference to the result, provided the alphabet is of size <math>q</math>.)

===Defining the bound===
Let <math>\ A_q(n,d)</math> denote the maximum possible size of a <math>q</math>-ary block code <math>\ C</math> of length <math>n</math> and minimum [[Hamming distance]] <math>d</math> between elements of the block code (necessarily positive for <math>q^n > 1</math>).

Then, the Hamming bound is:

:<math>
\ A_q(n,d) \leq \frac{q^n}{\sum_{k=0}^t \binom{n}{k}(q-1)^k}
</math>

where

:<math>t=\left\lfloor\frac{d-1}{2}\right\rfloor.</math>

==Proof==
It follows from the definition of <math>d</math> that if at most 
:<math> t = \left\lfloor\frac{1}{2}(d-1)\right\rfloor</math> 
errors are made during transmission of a codeword then [[minimum distance decoding]] will decode it correctly (i.e., it decodes the received word as the codeword that was sent). Thus the code is said to be capable of correcting <math>t</math> errors.

For each codeword <math>c \in C</math>, consider a [[ball (mathematics)|ball]] of fixed radius <math>t</math> around <math>c</math>. Every pair of these balls ([[Hamming ball]]s) are non-intersecting by the <math>t</math>-error-correcting property. Let <math>m</math> be the number of words in each ball (in other words, the volume of the ball). A word that is in such a ball can deviate in at most <math>t</math> components from those of the ball's [[ball (mathematics)|centre]], which is a codeword. The number of such words is then obtained by [[binomial coefficients|choosing]] up to <math>t</math> of the <math>n</math> components of a codeword to deviate to one of <math>(q-1)</math> possible other values (recall, the code is <math>q</math>-ary: it takes values in <math>\mathcal{A}_q^n</math>). Thus,

:<math>m =
 \begin{matrix}
  \sum_{k=0}^t \binom{n}{k}(q-1)^k
 \end{matrix}.</math>

<math>A_q (n,d)</math> is the (maximum) total number of codewords in <math>C</math>, and so, by the definition of <math>t</math>, the greatest number of balls with no two balls having a word in common. Taking the [[union (set theory)|union]] of the words in these balls centered at codewords, results in a set of words, each counted precisely once, that is a subset of <math>\mathcal{A}_q^n</math> (where <math>|\mathcal{A}_q^n| = q^n</math> words) and so:

:<math> A_q(n,d) \times m = A_q(n,d) \times
 \begin{matrix}
  \sum_{k=0}^t \binom{n}{k}(q-1)^k
 \end{matrix}
\leq q^n.</math>

Whence:

:<math>A_q(n,d) \leq \frac{q^n}{
 \begin{matrix}
  \sum_{k=0}^t \binom{n}{k}(q-1)^k
 \end{matrix}}.</math>

==Covering radius and packing radius==
:{{main|Delone set}}
For an <math>A_q(n,d)</math> code ''C'' (a subset of <math>\mathcal{A}_q^n</math>), the ''covering radius'' of ''C'' is the smallest value of ''r'' such that every element of <math>\mathcal{A}_q^n</math> is contained in at least one ball of radius ''r'' centered at each codeword of ''C''. The ''packing radius'' of ''C'' is the largest value of ''s'' such that the set of balls of radius ''s'' centered at each codeword of ''C'' are mutually [[disjoint sets|disjoint]].

From the proof of the Hamming bound, it can be seen that for <math> t\,=\,\left\lfloor\frac{1}{2}(d-1)\right\rfloor</math>, we have:
:: ''s'' ≤ ''t'' and ''t'' ≤ ''r''.
Therefore, ''s'' ≤ ''r'' and if equality holds then ''s'' = ''r'' = ''t''. The case of equality means that the Hamming bound is attained.

== Perfect codes ==
Codes that attain the Hamming bound are called '''perfect codes'''. Examples include codes that have only one codeword, and codes that are the whole of <math>\mathcal{A}_q^n</math>. Another example is given by the ''repeat codes'', where each symbol of the message is repeated an odd fixed number of times to obtain a codeword where ''q'' = 2. All of these examples are often called the ''trivial'' perfect codes.
In 1973, Tietäväinen proved{{Sfn|Tietäväinen|1973}} that any non-trivial perfect code over a prime-power alphabet has the parameters of a [[Hamming code]] or a [[Golay code (disambiguation)|Golay code]].

A perfect code may be interpreted as one in which the balls of Hamming radius ''t'' centered on codewords exactly fill out the space (''t'' is the covering radius = packing radius).  A '''quasi-perfect code''' is one in which the balls of Hamming radius ''t'' centered on codewords are disjoint and the balls of radius ''t''+1 cover the space, possibly with some overlaps.<ref>McWilliams and Sloane, p. 19</ref> Another way to say this is that a code is ''quasi-perfect'' if its covering radius is one greater than its packing radius.<ref>{{harvnb|Roman|1992|p=140}}</ref>
